attacks.claim: Automated SMS to about 142,000 people drawn from a purchased voter file, followed by three automated reminders, has no stated consent basis. That exposes the org to TCPA prior-express-consent risk and carrier 10DLC requirements, and voter-file use terms may restrict non-election use. STOP handling does not cure the initial unsolicited message.
attacks.evidence: "Load numbers into Twilio and send an automated SMS to every registered voter in the city (~142,000) with a link to the first poll, then 3 automated reminders over 10 days." ABSENT: consent capture, legal review, and County Clerk data-use terms.

attacks.claim: The weekly public CC-BY export publishes ward, zip, birth_year, gender, ranking, verified and created_at per response. In small wards or small polls these quasi-identifiers can single out individuals, and a CC-BY release cannot be recalled once mirrored. Removing resident_id does not prevent re-identification.
attacks.evidence: "one CSV per poll on data.ourtown.org with columns ward, zip, birth_year, gender, ranking, verified, created_at. resident_id is removed before export."

attacks.claim: Verified residents' birth_year, gender and zip were collected for jury-pool balance reports. Reusing them in a public export is a purpose change, and the plan states no notice or consent covering public release.
attacks.evidence: "collected at optional verification for the jury-pool-style demographic balance reports"

attacks.claim: No retention or deletion rules are stated for device fingerprints, IP logs, or imported voter-file mobile numbers, including numbers of non-responders. Fingerprinting also sits uneasily with an anonymous-first product.
attacks.evidence: "1 response per poll per device fingerprint" and "Load numbers into Twilio" with ABSENT: retention and deletion policy.

attacks.claim: The plan does not say whether verified poll_responses retain resident_id in the database. Stripping it only from the CSV leaves database-level linkability to residents unresolved, which bears on the anonymous-first claim.
attacks.evidence: "poll_responses(id, poll_id, resident_id null, ranking jsonb, ward, verified bool, created_at)"

attacks.claim: Instant-runoff behaviour is underspecified: tie-breaking, exhausted ballots, partial rankings, and whether verified and all-response columns are tallied separately or merged are all undefined. Council staff could contest published results.
attacks.evidence: "Live results page: instant-runoff rounds, split into "verified" and "all responses" columns."

attacks.claim: Per-ward results are the headline output, but ward is self-selected for unverified users. Anyone can skew a ward's tally, and there is no minimum sample or flag for thin wards.
attacks.evidence: "ward is self-selected for unverified users and derived from address for verified users."

attacks.claim: Device-fingerprint and per-IP limits are easily rotated or spoofed, so unverified headline tallies remain manipulable. The verified/unverified split labels brigading but does not prevent it.
attacks.evidence: "unverified responses over 3/min from one IP are queued for review."

attacks.claim: No write-path validation is described for ranking jsonb from untrusted clients, and no sanitisation is described for staff-authored option text rendered to residents.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: validation of ranking payloads and sanitisation of option text.

attacks.claim: Staff cannot edit or delete responses and options freeze at first response, so a mis-authored or abusive poll has no correction path. No data-subject deletion path is described either, which conflicts with deletion rights for personal fields.
attacks.evidence: "Staff cannot edit or delete responses; poll options are frozen once the first response arrives."

attacks.claim: Published CC-BY CSVs have no retraction, takedown, or correction process, and SMS sends cannot be recalled. The plan has no rollback for the two one-way outputs.
attacks.evidence: "Open-data export (weekly, public, CC-BY)" and the SMS send to "every registered voter".

attacks.claim: The centerpiece rests on the weakest survey signal. Polls scored 9%, while vote visibility scored 61% and notifications 44%, and the plan offers no evidence of demand for ranked-choice polling.
attacks.evidence: "Polls on upcoming items — 9%" vs. "Ward Voice ... is the centerpiece of the FY27 roadmap."

attacks.claim: The 6,000-response and 30%-new-resident targets have no derivation or baseline. The new-resident target depends on the SMS outreach that is itself blocked.
attacks.evidence: "6,000 poll responses in the first 30 days." and "30% of responses from residents not previously active on OurTown."

attacks.claim: No retry, failure handling, alerting, or kill switch is specified for the SMS pipeline, the live IRV results, or the Monday 07:00 PDF. A bad message or stuck send cannot be stopped.
attacks.evidence: "Week 4: open-data export, staff PDF, voter-file import + SMS pipeline." ABSENT: throttle, kill switch, retry policy, alerting.

attacks.claim: A 142,000-recipient SMS burst with a link will spike traffic on the ranking UI and on Twilio throughput. The load test targets only 5k concurrency and does not model this spike.
attacks.evidence: "load test (target 5k concurrent), launch"

attacks.claim: Roughly 570,000 SMS messages (initial send plus three reminders) have no per-message budget, cap, or owner. Only the $400 file fee is stated, so spend is effectively unbounded.
attacks.evidence: "Purchase the county voter registration file from the County Clerk ($400, includes mobile numbers where provided)."

attacks.claim: Authoring, resident UI, IRV, results, abuse controls, export, PDF, voter import, SMS and accessibility must be delivered by three people in five weeks. The riskiest items (export, PDF, voter import, SMS) are stacked in week 4 with no slack.
attacks.evidence: "Team: 2 backend, 1 frontend | Duration: 5 weeks"

attacks.claim: Results are framed as giving residents a direct voice on council decisions, but the plan gives no methodology or non-representativeness disclaimer for self-selected poll results presented to council or the public.
attacks.evidence: "Ward Voice gives residents a direct voice on the items council is actually deciding"

attacks.claim: Keyboard and screen-reader ranking behaviour is not specified, and the accessibility pass is compressed into a single week.
attacks.evidence: "resident ranking UI (mobile-first, drag or tap-to-rank)"

attacks.claim: Resident phone numbers and outbound messaging depend on one vendor (Twilio) and one source (County Clerk), with no exit path or data-residency terms described.
attacks.evidence: "Load numbers into Twilio"
